title: Why Do Japanese Oni Wear Tiger Skin?
subtitle: A hat on Mount Asakura, a one-eyed oni in Izumo, a word that may mean hidden, the ox-and-tiger explanation, and who was chased at Setsubun

segments.text: Picture an oni, a demon from Japanese folklore. Red or blue skin, horns on its head, a loincloth of tiger skin, and an iron club in its hand. That is how oni appear today, in picture books, at festivals, and every February at Setsubun, when families throw roasted beans to drive them out of the house. But the oldest Japanese records are still here. So, why do oni wear tiger skin? And did they always?

In this episode, we check four things that are often said about oni. That oni always looked like this. That the word oni means hidden. That the horns and the tiger skin come from a direction on the compass. And that oni are the ones who get chased away. One by one, we will hold each of them up against the old sources.

Japan's oldest official history, the Nihon Shoki, was completed in seven twenty. It is written in Chinese characters, and it uses the character that is read as oni today. In early Chinese writing, that character was tied to the spirits of the dead.

The chronicle tells of the year six sixty-one. Empress Saimei had moved her court to a temporary palace in Kyushu, in the west of Japan. That summer, she died there. Then, after the crown prince had brought her remains back to the Palace of Ihase, that evening, on the top of Mount Asakura, there was an oni. It wore a large hat, and it looked down on the funeral. Everyone who saw it cried out in wonder. When W. G. Aston translated this passage into English in eighteen ninety-six, he wrote demon, and added a note: or spirit. The chronicle says nothing about horns, tiger skin, or a club.

About seventy years after these events, in seven thirty-three, the province of Izumo completed a record of its land, the Izumo Fudoki. It explains the name of one village, Ayo, with a story. Long ago, a man was farming a mountain field. A one-eyed oni came and ate his son. The parents hid in a bamboo thicket, and the bamboo leaves stirred. As he was being eaten, the son cried out, ayo, ayo. And so the place was called Ayo.
So the first claim does not hold. In two of the oldest records, one oni wears a hat and watches in silence. The other has a single eye. Neither record mentions horns or tiger skin.

The second claim is about the word itself. In the nine thirties, the scholar Minamoto no Shitagou compiled a dictionary, the Wamyō Ruijushō. Under the character for oni, he gives the Japanese reading, oni. Then he adds a note. Some say that it comes from on, the sound of the character for hidden, because oni hide themselves and do not wish to show their form. The entry ends with a short definition: the soul of a person who has died.

So the idea is very old, more than a thousand years. But even then, it came with the words some say. It is an early guess, not a proven origin. In the Tales of Ise, a collection that took shape around the tenth century, a woman is carried off on a stormy night, and an oni swallows her in a single gulp. The tale never describes the oni. And a note at the end of the episode explains that the oni was really her own brothers, who had come to take her back.

Faces began to appear in pictures. In the Illustrated Legends of the Kitano Tenjin Shrine, a scroll painted in the late thirteenth century, strange figures with horns and wild hair gather by a gate. Over the following centuries, artists kept giving oni horns, fangs and fierce faces.

The third claim explains the horns and the tiger skin. In seventeen seventy-nine, the artist Toriyama Sekien published a book of monsters. Beside his oni, he wrote a short note. People call the northeast, the direction of the ox and the tiger, the demon gate. When oni are painted today, they wear the horns of an ox on their heads and the skin of a tiger around their waists. This shape, he says, is said to join the ox and the tiger together.

It is a neat explanation, and Sekien himself presents it as something people say. He wrote it down more than a thousand years after the oldest records, and about five hundred years after the horned figures in the Kitano scroll. Whether the picture or the explanation came first, the sources do not tell us.

The last claim brings us back to Setsubun. A court rite to drive away disease is recorded in seven oh six, in a year when many people died. In a later court manual, the Gōke Shidai, from about nine hundred years ago, an official called the hōsō leads the rite. He shouts, strikes his shield three times with his spear, and the courtiers join in the cry and chase. Then the manual adds one more line: the courtiers shoot arrows at the hōsō. Beans came later. In fourteen forty-seven, a Zen monk wrote down the cry, oni out, fortune in, and called it the way demons were driven out in this land.
So the roles changed. In that court manual, the figure who led the chase also became a target. And by the fifteenth century, beans were being thrown, and the oni was the one sent outside.

So, why do oni wear tiger skin? One explanation links it to the ox and the tiger, the unlucky northeast. Sekien recorded it in seventeen seventy-nine, long after the first oni. The oldest records show something else: a figure in a large hat on a mountain, a one-eyed creature in a mountain field, and a word that may mean hidden. The horns, the tiger skin and the club came later, through pictures.
Every story has an origin. Sometimes, it begins with something no one could see.
